meta.title: Stock Split vs. Reverse Split: Shares, Price & Acquisition Cost
meta.heading: Stock Split vs. Reverse Split: Shares, Price & Acquisition Cost
meta.description: Compare forward and reverse splits on the same holding. Reconcile share quantity, proportional price and average acquisition cost without inventing a gain.
meta.cardIntro: Use the same starting shares, reference price and average cost to isolate the new-for-old ratio. The split changes per-share amounts; issuer settlement terms and subsequent market trading remain separate.

stock-split.intro: Use the same starting shares, reference price and average cost to isolate the new-for-old ratio. The split changes per-share amounts; issuer settlement terms and subsequent market trading remain separate.
stock-split.answer: A forward split and a reverse split apply reciprocal quantity and per-share adjustments to the same holding. For 120 initial shares, 3-for-2 produces 180 theoretical shares while 1-for-10 produces 12. Both retain the same $5,400 proportional reference value and $3,600 entered total acquisition cost.

sections.title: How do I enter forward and reverse split ratios?
paragraphs: Read the ratio as new shares for old shares. Three new for two old gives a factor of 1.5; one new for ten old gives 0.1. Multiply initial quantity by that factor and divide each initial per-share reference amount by it. The same convention handles either direction without a separate formula.

Keep quantity and reference price from the same pre-event position. Mixing an already adjusted price with an unadjusted share count applies part of the action twice. Confirm the event’s effective date and eligibility outside this worksheet; entering a ratio does not establish that a holding qualifies.

sections.title: Does a split change the amount invested?
paragraphs: For an intact position with no settlement or fee, proportional reallocation leaves total acquisition cost unchanged. In the example, 120 shares times $30 cost and 180 shares times $20 cost both equal $3,600. This is a mathematical reconciliation rather than an increase in wealth.

The corresponding $5,400 reference value is 120 times $45 before and 180 times $30 after. Real trading prices can move for other reasons. The calculator keeps that market movement out of the split adjustment instead of describing a higher share count as a realized profit.

sections.title: What happens to fractional entitlements?
paragraphs: A 1-for-10 reverse split on 103 shares gives a theoretical entitlement of 10.3 shares. At a $4 original reference price, the proportional price is $40 and reference value remains $412. Keeping the fraction exposes the full arithmetic before an issuer’s settlement policy is applied.

Some arrangements round or replace fractions with cash, and the price used for that payment can differ from the proportional reference price. This tool does not choose a policy or calculate taxable gains from a cash settlement. Use the actual corporate-action notice and broker records for those amounts.

sections.title: How should multiple splits be combined?
paragraphs: Multiply the ratios in chronological order and inspect the intermediate quantities. A 3-for-2 split followed by 1-for-5 has a cumulative factor of 0.3. Starting with 120 shares therefore gives 36 theoretical shares. A $45 reference price becomes $150, preserving the same $5,400 reference value.

The sequence assumes the position stays intact between events. Purchases, sales, transfers, fees and fractional cash settlements can alter that reconciliation. Record those as separate transactions rather than forcing them into another split ratio. The average-cost illustration also does not select an authorized tax-basis method.

sections.title: Forward and reverse ratios preserve the same reference totals
paragraphs: Both cases begin with 120 shares, a $45 reference price and $30 average acquisition cost per share. Only the ratio changes: 3-for-2 or 1-for-10. Theoretical fractions are retained, and no trade or cash-in-lieu event is modeled.

questions.question: Why does the reverse-split reference price rise while shares fall?
questions.answer: Quantity is multiplied by the new-for-old factor while proportional price divides by it. Those reciprocal changes preserve the intact holding’s reference value.

questions.question: Does an unchanged total acquisition cost establish my completed tax basis?
questions.answer: No. The example allocates an entered average cost across an intact position. Tax lots, fees, sales and fractional cash settlements can require additional records.

questions.question: When should I consult the issuer or broker notice?
questions.answer: Use it for ratio direction, eligibility, record and effective dates, rounding and cash-in-lieu treatment. The arithmetic does not infer those terms.

meta.title: CAC vs. ROAS: New Customers, Cost Scope & Attribution
meta.heading: CAC vs. ROAS: New Customers, Cost Scope & Attribution
meta.description: Compare cost per unique new customer with revenue per advertising dollar. Separate full-scope CAC, advertising-only cost and ROAS before judging efficiency.
meta.cardIntro: CAC uses unique new customers as its denominator, while ROAS uses advertising spend. The examples keep their distinct cost and revenue scopes visible so a smaller-looking number is not mistaken for better profitability.

customer-acquisition-cost.intro: CAC uses unique new customers as its denominator, while ROAS uses advertising spend. The examples keep their distinct cost and revenue scopes visible so a smaller-looking number is not mistaken for better profitability.
customer-acquisition-cost.answer: CAC is cost per unique new customer; ROAS is attributed revenue per advertising dollar. The defined cohort gives $250 full-scope CAC or $120 advertising-only cost per customer, while a separately specified revenue figure gives 3-times ROAS. These units and scopes do not substitute for customer profit.

sections.title: Which customer count belongs in CAC?
paragraphs: Count each customer once when first acquired under your stated definition. A lead, trial sign-up, order and repeat purchase can all represent different events. Choose the customer event and the population before dividing cost. The worksheet asks for whole unique new customers rather than silently treating orders as people or accounts.

For example, if the 100 newly acquired customers place 150 orders, the matched CAC remains $25,000 divided by 100, or $250. Dividing by 150 would produce cost per order under that scope. It could be useful separately, but labeling it CAC would conceal the changed denominator.

sections.title: Which costs should I include without double counting?
paragraphs: Known-total mode accepts a reconciled acquisition amount. Itemized mode adds your nonoverlapping advertising, personnel, agency, software and other allocated costs. Shared resources require a defensible allocation to acquisition rather than automatic inclusion of every company expense or complete exclusion of employee time.

One example allocates $12,000 advertising, $8,000 personnel and $5,000 other acquisition costs, totaling $25,000. If an agency invoice already contains media spend, do not add that same media amount as advertising again. A paid-ad-only figure is narrower than fully loaded acquisition cost and should keep that label.

sections.title: How do time lag and channel attribution affect the result?
paragraphs: Use a consistent period, currency, acquisition event and attribution population. A long sales cycle can separate the cost date from the customer’s first purchase. A simple same-month ratio may then differ from a cohort analysis. Enter a scope that fits the decision and retain it when comparing periods.

The calculator does not decide which channel caused a sale or reconcile delayed conversions. It also does not infer customers from platform conversion counts. Comparing one channel’s narrow paid-acquisition figure with another channel’s fully allocated CAC can produce a misleading ranking even when both divisions are correct.

sections.title: How should CAC be compared with ROAS and profit?
paragraphs: ROAS uses attributed revenue over advertising spend. CAC uses acquisition costs over new customers. The numerator and denominator differ in both cases. Neither metric alone includes every product cost, fixed expense, retention cost or future customer behavior needed to establish profit.

With zero new customers, CAC has no defined denominator. With zero included cost and positive new customers, the arithmetic is zero, which can signal omitted costs. An LTV comparison needs a separately supported customer-value model; this worksheet does not invent a universal healthy ratio or an approved ad budget.

sections.title: Keep dollars per customer separate from a revenue-to-ad-spend multiple
paragraphs: The CAC cases use 100 unique new customers, $12,000 advertising and either $13,000 additional acquisition costs or no additional costs. The separate ROAS illustration assumes $36,000 attributed revenue on that $12,000 ad spend. Revenue is not assumed to come exclusively from those new customers, so this is a measure-definition comparison rather than a complete customer-profit analysis.

questions.question: Can a campaign have attractive ROAS and still have high CAC?
questions.answer: Yes. The measures use different numerators, denominators and attribution scopes. Advertising revenue efficiency does not capture every acquisition cost or the new-customer count.

questions.question: Why does advertising-only cost per customer differ from all-in CAC?
questions.answer: It omits the allocated personnel and other included acquisition costs. Keep the definition consistent before interpreting the difference as an improvement.

questions.question: What additional information is needed to discuss customer profitability?
questions.answer: Examine contribution or gross profit, retention, acquisition-cost scope and timing with reliable customer cohorts. CAC and ROAS alone do not establish lifetime profit.

meta.title: Dividend Discount Model vs. Reinvestment: Value, D0/D1 & Growth
meta.heading: Dividend Discount Model vs. Reinvestment: Value, D0/D1 & Growth
meta.description: Distinguish dividend-discount value from reinvestment growth. Test required-return sensitivity on one dividend stream without treating either output as a forecast.
meta.cardIntro: A dividend-discount model asks what an assumed distribution stream is worth at a chosen required return. A reinvestment projection asks how holdings might accumulate under price, dividend and reinvestment assumptions. Their outputs answer different questions.

dividend-discount-model.intro: A dividend-discount model asks what an assumed distribution stream is worth at a chosen required return. A reinvestment projection asks how holdings might accumulate under price, dividend and reinvestment assumptions. Their outputs answer different questions.
dividend-discount-model.answer: Dividend-discount valuation estimates present value at a chosen required return; a reinvestment projection estimates an accumulation path under additional assumptions. For the same $2 latest dividend and 4% growth, reducing required return from 10% to 8% changes the stable-growth value from about $34.67 to $52. Neither value forecasts a market price.

sections.title: Why does the D0 or D1 choice change valuation?
paragraphs: D0 denotes the latest annual dividend, while D1 denotes the next expected annual dividend. In stable-growth mode, D0 is multiplied once by one plus growth. A known D1 is used directly. Applying growth to an already forward dividend shifts the entire perpetual stream and overstates its value under the chosen assumptions.

For a constant $3 next annual dividend and 8% required return, zero growth gives $37.50 per share. This is a perpetual end-period model. A near-term one-off distribution or an irregular calendar needs a cash-flow representation that preserves its actual timing rather than this simplified annual stream.

sections.title: Why must required return exceed perpetual growth?
paragraphs: The Gordon construction requires a positive return-minus-growth spread for the stated convergent perpetual stream. At 10% return and 4% growth, that spread is six percentage points. It is a subtraction of rates, not their ratio. Equal or higher perpetual growth does not justify a negative or infinite displayed stock price.

Values become highly sensitive as the positive spread narrows. Small changes in a difficult-to-support perpetual assumption can dominate the result. The worksheet checks mathematical validity, but it does not establish that a firm can sustain the entered growth or that the required return is appropriate.

sections.title: Where does a two-stage terminal value belong?
paragraphs: The early stage grows D0 for N full annual periods. The first stable-stage dividend is D(N+1). Divide that dividend by the required return minus stable growth to obtain the terminal price at N, then discount that terminal price by N periods. Add the present values of dividends from years one through N.

For D0 $2, two years of 10% growth, subsequent 3% growth and 8% required return, early dividends are $2.20 and $2.42. Terminal price at year two is $49.852. Its present value plus the early dividend present values gives $46.851852 per share. The tool applies one required return across both stages.

sections.title: How is discount valuation different from dividend reinvestment?
paragraphs: A DRIP projection follows share purchases and reinvested distributions under assumed future share prices. DDM instead discounts assumed future dividends to obtain a model value today. A larger ending DRIP account is not automatically evidence that the stock’s current price is below a defensible DDM value.

A zero dividend with proportional growth stays zero in this worksheet. That is a limitation of the supplied distribution path, not proof that a non-dividend-paying company has no market value. Payout changes, future profitability, buybacks and other capital policies require a different or expanded valuation analysis.

sections.title: The same dividend stream can have different assumed present values
paragraphs: Both cases use a latest annual dividend of $2 and perpetual growth of 4%. Only the entered required return changes, from 10% to 8%. Neither value is a market quote, a recommendation to buy or a dividend-growth forecast.

questions.question: Why is DDM value not a projected future account balance?
questions.answer: It discounts an assumed dividend stream to the valuation date. It does not simulate purchases, reinvestment prices or the number of shares accumulated.

questions.question: Why does a smaller required-return spread raise the modeled value so much?
questions.answer: The Gordon formula divides the next dividend by required return minus perpetual growth. A small denominator makes the result especially sensitive to the assumptions.

questions.question: Can I compare a DRIP ending balance directly with DDM fair value?
questions.answer: Not as the same measure. Align valuation date, invested capital, share quantity and assumptions, then distinguish present-value analysis from an accumulation projection.

meta.title: Basic EPS vs. Diluted EPS: Earnings Scope & Weighted Shares
meta.heading: Basic EPS vs. Diluted EPS: Earnings Scope & Weighted Shares
meta.description: Compare basic EPS denominators and identify what diluted EPS additionally requires. Reconcile common earnings and period-weighted shares without hidden dilution.
meta.cardIntro: First calculate common earnings and a valid weighted share denominator for basic EPS. Then identify the separate instrument-specific adjustments needed for diluted EPS; the worksheet does not manufacture a diluted result from a simple extra-share input.

earnings-per-share.intro: First calculate common earnings and a valid weighted share denominator for basic EPS. Then identify the separate instrument-specific adjustments needed for diluted EPS; the worksheet does not manufacture a diluted result from a simple extra-share input.
earnings-per-share.answer: Basic EPS requires common earnings and an appropriately weighted common-share denominator. Diluted EPS adds separate instrument-specific and anti-dilution analysis. The two checked cases below are both basic EPS; their $3 and $5.1328125 results reflect different share histories, not an automatically calculated dilution adjustment.

sections.title: Which earnings belong to common shareholders?
paragraphs: Match the income period and ownership scope with the shares in the denominator. This simplified worksheet starts from net income and subtracts a preferred earnings adjustment that you have already checked. That adjustment is not a request for every dividend paid; ordinary common-share dividends do not reduce the earnings numerator in this step.

Preferred rights, cumulative amounts, participating securities and other allocation rules can require more work than a simple cash-dividend subtraction. The worksheet makes the entered adjustment visible rather than inferring those rules. It does not claim to prepare a complete US GAAP or IFRS earnings-per-share disclosure.

sections.title: Why is an ending share count insufficient?
paragraphs: An issuance or buyback changes the number of shares participating for different portions of the earnings period. Basic EPS therefore uses a weighted average for the selected period. Known-average mode accepts a previously reconciled amount; it does not assume an ending balance is representative.

In the schedule example, 100,000 shares for 90 days and 200,000 for 275 days cover a 365-day period. The weighted average is 175,342.465753 shares. Dividing $900,000 common earnings by that amount gives $5.1328125 EPS. The tool checks that the entered whole-day segment lengths sum to the full period.

sections.title: How do share events and losses affect the worksheet?
paragraphs: Enter shares outstanding during each segment, not just newly issued shares. The segments should cover the period without gaps or overlaps. Split, consolidation and bonus-share restatements may require a consistently revised historical schedule; those accounting adjustments must already be reflected in the supplied data.

A loss is preserved. For a $100,000 net loss, a $10,000 entered preferred adjustment and 50,000 weighted shares, basic EPS is negative $2.20. Zero weighted shares make EPS undefined. Turning that state into a real zero would hide the missing denominator rather than report a usable earnings measure.

sections.title: Why does basic EPS not automatically give diluted EPS?
paragraphs: Diluted EPS can require both earnings and share-count adjustments for potential common shares. Convertibles, options, warrants and contingently issuable shares have different mechanics. Anti-dilution treatment can also affect which instruments belong in a loss-period calculation.

The current calculator computes basic EPS only. Its companion explanation distinguishes the additional diluted task instead of implying that any user-entered extra share amount produces an accounting-compliant diluted result. EPS is a period profit-per-share measure, not a stock price, payout promise or personal investment return.

sections.title: Two basic EPS cases with different share histories
paragraphs: Both cases use $1 million net income less a $100,000 preferred earnings adjustment. One assumes 300,000 weighted average common shares; the other weights 100,000 shares for 90 days and 200,000 for 275 days. Both outputs are basic EPS. The different historical denominator is not a diluted-EPS calculation.

questions.question: Is the weighted-schedule result a diluted EPS figure?
questions.answer: No. It is basic EPS using shares outstanding during each period segment. Potential common-share instruments and their earnings adjustments are a separate task.

questions.question: Why not divide by the final day’s share count?
questions.answer: An ending balance does not reflect how long shares were outstanding. Use an appropriately restated, period-weighted denominator for the analysis.

questions.question: What extra work can diluted EPS require?
questions.answer: Potential common shares can require both numerator and denominator adjustments, with instrument-specific and anti-dilution treatment. The basic worksheet does not determine that accounting result.

meta.title: Sharpe Ratio vs. Total Return: Excess Returns, Volatility & Time
meta.heading: Sharpe Ratio vs. Total Return: Excess Returns, Volatility & Time
meta.description: Compare Sharpe ratio and compounded return for controlled monthly sequences. Separate arithmetic excess return, sample volatility and reinvestment growth.
meta.cardIntro: Sharpe relates arithmetic excess return to volatility; compounded total return follows the product of period growth factors. The paired four-observation sequences show why neither output substitutes for the other.

sharpe-ratio.intro: Sharpe relates arithmetic excess return to volatility; compounded total return follows the product of period growth factors. The paired four-observation sequences show why neither output substitutes for the other.
sharpe-ratio.answer: Sharpe uses arithmetic excess return divided by volatility, while total return compounds period growth factors. The two controlled monthly sequences share a 0.5% arithmetic mean but have different volatility, Sharpe ratios and compounded returns. A higher ratio in this short sample is not a future-performance conclusion.

sections.title: Why subtract a matching-period risk-free return?
paragraphs: Sharpe ratio uses a differential or excess return, rather than the investment return alone. With a constant risk-free return for each observation, subtracting that constant changes the mean but not the standard deviation. If the benchmark varies, the volatility must describe the actual excess-return series.

Keep monthly returns, monthly risk-free return and monthly volatility together, or use a consistently annual set. The tool does not convert an annual input into a monthly one silently. It also does not substitute CAGR for the arithmetic average of the observation-period returns.

sections.title: What does the return-series mode calculate?
paragraphs: Enter equally spaced simple percentage returns rather than stock prices or dollar profits. A value of 1 means 1%, not one dollar or a decimal return of one. The worksheet subtracts the fixed same-period risk-free return, computes the mean and uses n−1 for the sample variance denominator.

For monthly returns −2%, 1%, 3% and 0% with zero monthly risk-free return, the mean is 0.5% and sample deviation is about 2.081666%. Period Sharpe is 0.240192. The sample contains four observations, not a full year; choosing twelve periods per year supplies an annualization assumption rather than additional evidence.

sections.title: When does square-root annualization apply?
paragraphs: The displayed annualized illustration multiplies period Sharpe by the square root of the entered periods per year. For the sample above and twelve periods, the result is 0.832050. A factor of one leaves already annual statistics unchanged. A 252-period trading-year choice is an explicit assumption, not an automatically read exchange calendar.

Square-root scaling relies on stable moments and zero serial correlation under an additive aggregation construction. Compounding and autocorrelation can change the relationship. The tool labels this as an assumption-based illustration and does not claim to estimate autocorrelation, correct it, or produce an exact geometric annual return.

sections.title: What do negative or undefined results tell me?
paragraphs: Negative mean excess return produces a negative Sharpe ratio when volatility is positive. It is not squared into a positive score. Zero excess-return volatility leaves the ratio undefined even when the mean is nonzero. Very small volatility or a short sample can also produce unstable estimates.

Sharpe is different from total profit, CAGR, beta and a guaranteed future return. Compare compatible fees, distribution treatment, periods and benchmark conventions. This worksheet does not turn one ratio into a universal good/bad rating or select an investment on the user’s behalf.

sections.title: Equal arithmetic averages do not imply equal Sharpe or compounded return
paragraphs: Both hypothetical monthly sequences have a 0.5% arithmetic mean and zero monthly risk-free return. Sequence A is −2%, 1%, 3%, 0%; Sequence B is 0%, 0%, 1%, 1%. The total-return column separately compounds those returns with no cash flows, fees or taxes. Four observations and a chosen 12-period scaling factor are not evidence of a full year’s performance.

questions.question: Why do the sequences have different Sharpe ratios despite matching average returns?
questions.answer: Their sample volatilities differ. Sharpe divides arithmetic mean excess return by that volatility, so the same mean can support different ratios.

questions.question: Why does compounded total return differ from the arithmetic average?
questions.answer: Total growth multiplies period growth factors. An arithmetic mean is a different summary and does not account for the same compounding path.

questions.question: Does the larger ratio identify a superior future investment?
questions.answer: No. The sample, benchmark, fees, distribution treatment and scaling assumptions matter. These controlled sequences do not establish a forecast or a universal ranking rule.

meta.title: Option Theoretical Value vs. Expiration Payoff: Black-Scholes Inputs
meta.heading: Option Theoretical Value vs. Expiration Payoff: Black-Scholes Inputs
meta.description: Compare European option model value before expiry with zero-time intrinsic value. Keep spot assumptions, trade premium and profit separate.
meta.cardIntro: The comparison holds hypothetical spot and strike fixed while changing time remaining. It isolates a model relationship, rather than predicting how an actual option or stock price will evolve.

black-scholes.intro: The comparison holds hypothetical spot and strike fixed while changing time remaining. It isolates a model relationship, rather than predicting how an actual option or stock price will evolve.
black-scholes.answer: European option value before expiry differs from intrinsic payoff at expiry and from a trade’s profit. With the stated $100 spot and strike, the one-year model gives about $10.450584 call value and $5.573526 put value per share; at expiry with the same assumed spot, both intrinsic values are zero. A trade profit would also need its actual premium and costs.

sections.title: Which units and rates does the model require?
paragraphs: Spot and strike are dollars per share. Volatility is annualized and entered as a percentage. The risk-free rate and dividend yield are annual continuously compounded rates: enter 5 for 5%, which becomes 0.05 internally. An effective annual return or a simple borrowing APR is not automatically the same rate.

Time can be entered directly in years or as calendar days divided by 365. The latter is an explicit model day-count convention. It does not infer a trading-day calendar, an exchange expiration timestamp or an overnight market update. Keep all parameters on the same valuation basis.

sections.title: Why are theoretical value, payoff and profit different?
paragraphs: Before expiry, the model prices future contingent exercise under its assumptions. At expiry, a call’s intrinsic value is the positive part of spot minus strike; a put reverses that difference. A purchased option’s profit also subtracts the premium paid and fees, while a written strategy has its own collateral and stock exposure.

The displayed values are per share. A contract multiplier and contract count would be needed to form a contract total; those quantities are not assumed here. Use the covered-call or cash-secured-put calculator for an explicit expiration-position scenario instead of treating a theoretical price as net trading profit.

sections.title: What does the continuous dividend assumption change?
paragraphs: The model discounts spot by exp(−qT) and strike by exp(−rT). In the same $100/$100 one-year example with 3% continuous dividend yield, call value is about $8.652529 and put value $6.730918. Those inputs represent a continuous yield assumption rather than a list of dated cash distributions.

Put-call parity reconciles the two prices with discounted spot minus discounted strike. A small residual is a floating-point consistency check, not proof of an available arbitrage. Bid/ask spreads, financing, transaction costs, actual distributions and exercise terms are outside this worksheet.

sections.title: How are expiry, zero volatility and American exercise handled?
paragraphs: At zero remaining time, the tool returns intrinsic value. At zero volatility with positive time, it uses the deterministic discounted spot/strike difference. A negative continuous risk-free rate is permitted; it does not trigger a forced zero price. The spot table changes only spot while holding the remaining assumptions fixed.

This model is limited to European exercise and a continuous dividend yield. It does not price American early exercise or produce an accounting valuation for an employee grant. Constant volatility and rates are modeling assumptions. No live price, exercise recommendation or probability of assignment is inferred from the result.

questions.question: Why can a call have positive model value when spot equals strike before expiry?
questions.answer: Time remains for contingent future outcomes under the model. At expiry with the same assumed spot and strike, intrinsic value is zero; that is a different time condition.

questions.question: Does theoretical value equal the profit from buying an option?
questions.answer: No. Profit also depends on the premium actually paid, fees, contract size and the eventual outcome or closing price. A model value alone contains none of that completed trade history.

questions.question: Can this comparison price American early exercise or dated cash dividends?
questions.answer: No. The calculation uses European exercise, constant volatility and continuous rates and yield. Different exercise or dividend structures require other treatment.
